title: Organic Chemistry: Some Basic Principles and Techniques
tagline: How organic molecules are drawn, named, classified and purified, and how reaction mechanisms are read.

overview.intro: Organic chemistry is the chemistry of carbon compounds, and its vastness is made manageable by a small number of principles. This unit introduces the tetravalence of carbon and the shapes that follow from it, the structural representations and classification schemes used to describe organic molecules, the IUPAC nomenclature that gives every compound one unambiguous name, and the concept of isomerism. It then opens the machinery of reaction mechanisms — how bonds break, which electrons move and what intermediate forms — before turning to the practical techniques by which a crude product is purified and analysed, including the calculation of percentage composition and molecular formula from combustion data.

learningOutcomes: Draw and interpret the Lewis, condensed and bond-line structures of organic compounds and relate hybridisation to shape.
Classify organic compounds and apply the IUPAC rules of nomenclature to give correct, unambiguous names.
Distinguish structural, positional and chain isomerism and the stereoisomerism of geometrical isomers.
Explain fission, electron-displacement effects and the common intermediates, and describe the purification and analysis of organic compounds.
Draw the Lewis structure of ethene, identify every bond as σ or π, and use sp² hybridisation to explain why the molecule is planar and why rotation about the double bond is restricted.
Use Carius method results to calculate the percentage of a halogen in an organic compound from the mass of the silver halide obtained.

learn.title: General introduction, tetravalence and structural representations

blocks.text: Carbon is unique in forming an enormous number of compounds because of three properties: its tetravalence lets it form four bonds, its atomic size is small so the bonds are strong, and its ability to bond to itself — catenation — lets chains and rings of almost any length build up. The four bonds of carbon are formed by sp³, sp² or sp hybridisation, giving tetrahedral (109.5°), trigonal planar (120°) and linear (180°) geometries respectively, and because carbon can also form multiple bonds and bonds to every other element except the noble gases, the range of structures is essentially unlimited. Organic compounds are divided into open-chain or acyclic compounds, in which the carbon atoms form straight or branched chains, and cyclic compounds, which are further split into carbocycles containing only carbon in the ring and heterocycles containing at least one other atom.

Structures are drawn at four levels of detail. The complete Lewis structure shows every bond as a line and every atom with its lone pairs, which is accurate but cluttered. The condensed structural formula groups atoms without drawing bonds, as CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃, and the bond-line or skeleton formula draws only the carbon skeleton as zig-zag lines with hydrogens implied: a hexagon with a circle inside is benzene, and each vertex or terminus is understood to carry enough hydrogens to give carbon four bonds. Bond-line formulas are what research chemists actually use because they show the shape of the molecule at a glance, and reading them fluently is one of the first practical skills of the subject.

items.text: Write the bond-line formula of butan-2-ol and say what each vertex carries.
items.note: A zig-zag of four carbon positions with an -OH group drawn on the second vertex. Carbon 1 (a terminus) carries three hydrogens, carbon 2 carries the OH and one hydrogen, carbon 3 carries two hydrogens, and carbon 4 carries three: CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃.

items.text: Write the complete Lewis structure of ethene, C₂H₄, including every lone pair, and state what hybridisation the carbon atoms must have.
items.note: Each carbon forms four bonds in total, two to the other carbon and two to hydrogen. Ethene has no lone pairs, so the Lewis structure is H₂C=CH₂: draw two carbons side by side, double-bond them, and attach two hydrogens to each, with a total of six atoms and four C−H single bonds, one C=C double bond, and no lone pairs on any atom. Both carbon atoms are coplanar and every H−C−H bond angle is about 117°, which is the geometry expected of sp² hybridisation: two of the three sp² orbitals overlap with two hydrogen 1s orbitals, the third overlaps with the sp² orbital of the other carbon to form the σ bond, and the remaining unhybridised p orbitals on the two carbons overlap sideways to form the π bond that makes the double bond. The student should be able to identify why the molecule is planar and why rotation about the double bond is restricted, since breaking the π overlap is required to turn one eclipsed conformer into another.

items.meaning: The ability of an element, especially carbon, to bond to itself and form long chains and rings.
A skeletal drawing in which each vertex and line end is a carbon atom and hydrogens are implied.
An atom or group of atoms that determines the characteristic chemical reactions of a compound.

blocks.text: Organic compounds are classified structurally as saturated (only single bonds), unsaturated (at least one multiple bond), aliphatic (open-chain or alicyclic) and aromatic (benzene-like). Functionally they are grouped by the functional group they carry: alcohols hold -OH, aldehydes -CHO, ketones >C=O, carboxylic acids -COOH, amines -NH₂, halides -X, and hydrocarbons are themselves classified as alkanes, alkenes, alkynes and arenes. Each family has a characteristic suffix — -ane, -ene, -yne, -ol, -al, -one, -oic acid — so the name of a compound tells its family before any structure is drawn.

IUPAC nomenclature follows a fixed sequence of rules. Choose the longest continuous carbon chain that contains the principal functional group; that chain gives the root word and the number of carbons (meth 1, eth 2, prop 3, but 4, pent 5, hex 6, hept 7, oct 8, non 9, dec 10). Number from the end that gives the principal functional group the lowest locant, and if there is no functional group, the lowest set of locants for substituents. Name the substituents as prefixes with their position numbers, list them alphabetically ignoring prefixes such as di and tri, and assemble the name as prefix-root-suffix. Thus CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃ is 2-methylbutane, CH₃CH₂CH(OH)CH₃ is butan-2-ol, and (CH₃)₂CHCH=CH₂ is 3-methylbut-1-ene. Common names persist in practice — acetic acid for ethanoic acid, formic acid for methanoic acid, acetone for propanone — so both systems should be recognised.

blocks.caption: The IUPAC skeleton: root words and family suffixes

blocks.text: Isomers are compounds with the same molecular formula but different structures, and they fall into two broad classes. Structural isomerism differs in the connectivity of the atoms: chain isomerism changes the carbon skeleton, as in butane and 2-methylpropane (isobutane), both C₄H₁₀; position isomerism moves a functional group or multiple bond, as in propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol; and functional group isomerism changes the family altogether, as in ethanol and dimethyl ether, both C₂H₆O, or in propanoic acid and methyl ethanoate, both C₃H₆O₂. Metamerism is a further subtype found in ethers and ketones, where the same functional group sits between different alkyl groups on either side.

Stereoisomerism differs in the spatial arrangement rather than the connectivity. Geometrical isomerism arises when rotation about a bond is restricted, which in practice means a carbon-carbon double bond or a ring. But-2-ene exists as cis-but-2-ene, with both methyl groups on the same side and a dipole moment, and trans-but-2-ene, with them on opposite sides and a smaller dipole moment; the two have different boiling points and cannot be interconverted without breaking the π bond. Optical isomerism, met in compounds with a chiral carbon carrying four different groups, produces enantiomers that rotate plane-polarised light in opposite directions — a topic the course introduces qualitatively here.

items.text: Write all the isomers of C₄H₁₀ and name them by IUPAC.
items.note: There are two: the straight chain CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃, named butane, and the branched chain (CH₃)₃CH, named 2-methylpropane. Both are saturated open-chain alkanes, so they are chain isomers of each other, differing only in the skeleton and not in the functional group.

items.text: How many structural isomers does C₃H₈O contain?
items.note: Three: propan-1-ol (CH₃CH₂CH₂OH), propan-2-ol (CH₃CH(OH)CH₃) and methoxyethane (CH₃OCH₂CH₃). The first two are position isomers of the alcohol family, while the third is a functional-group isomer — an ether with the same molecular formula.

learn.title: Fundamental concepts in organic reaction mechanisms

blocks.text: A reaction mechanism is the step-by-step account of how reactant molecules become products, starting with how a covalent bond breaks. Homolytic fission divides the shared pair equally, giving one electron to each atom and producing two free radicals — highly reactive species with an unpaired electron, written with a single-headed (fish-hook) arrow. Heterolytic fission gives both electrons of the pair to the more electronegative atom, producing a carbocation (C⁺, electron deficient, electrophilic) and a carbanion (C⁻, electron rich, nucleophilic) or, when a halogen leaves, a halide ion. Ionic intermediates are more common in the reactions the course examines, because they are stabilised by solvation and by neighbouring groups.

Electrons then move in four recognised ways. The inductive effect is the permanent, through-bond transmission of charge: an electronegative substituent such as chlorine pulls electron density along the chain, with the effect falling off sharply over about three bonds; it is designated +I for electron-donating alkyl groups and −I for electron-withdrawing groups such as -NO₂ and -CN. The resonance or mesomeric effect is the delocalisation of π electrons over three or more adjacent atoms and is always stronger than the inductive effect; structures differing only in the position of π electrons are resonance contributors, and the real molecule is their hybrid. The electromeric effect is a temporary, complete transfer of a π pair towards an attacking reagent at the moment of reaction, denoted +C or −C. Hyperconjugation is the delocalisation of a σ bond (usually C–H) of an alkyl group into an adjacent empty or partially filled p orbital or π bond, and it explains why more substituted alkenes and carbocations are more stable — the famous stability order 3° > 2° > 1° > methyl.

Reagents are classified by the site they attack. A nucleophile (nucleus-loving) is an electron-rich species seeking a positive centre — OH⁻, CN⁻, NH₃ and halide ions are nucleophiles, and reactions they start are nucleophilic substitution or addition. An electrophile (electron-loving) is electron deficient and accepts an electron pair — H⁺, NO₂⁺ and BF₃ are electrophiles, and their reactions are electrophilic substitution or addition. Every mechanism is then read as a sequence: identify the attacking species, draw the electron-flow arrows from electron-rich to electron-poor, decide which intermediate forms, and finally remove a proton or a leaving group to give the product. The substitution of methane by chlorine proceeds through radicals (a free-radical substitution), whereas the nitration of benzene proceeds through the nitronium ion (an electrophilic substitution); recognising which family a reaction belongs to is the central skill of this lesson.

learn.title: Purification and analysis of organic compounds

blocks.text: A newly prepared organic compound is almost always contaminated, and the technique chosen depends on the physical property that differs from the impurity. Crystallisation dissolves the solid in a minimum of hot solvent and lets pure crystals form on cooling, leaving soluble impurities in the mother liquor; sublimation separates substances that pass directly from solid to vapour, such as camphor or naphthalene, from non-volatile impurities. Distillation separates liquids by boiling point — simple distillation for liquids that differ by more than about 25 °C or that are dissolved in a non-volatile solid, fractional distillation for closer-boiling mixtures using a fractionating column, and distillation under reduced pressure for liquids that decompose near their boiling point. Differential extraction moves a solute between two immiscible solvents, and chromatography separates components by their differing adsorption on a stationary phase — the basis of paper and thin-layer chromatography, in which each component is identified by its retardation factor Rf.

Analysis establishes what the purified compound contains. Qualitative analysis detects the elements present: the sodium fusion test converts covalently bound nitrogen, sulphur and halogen into ionic sodium cyanide, sodium sulphide and sodium halide, which are then detected by Prussian blue for nitrogen, lead acetate blackening for sulphur, and silver nitrate precipitates for halogens. Quantitative analysis measures them. In the Duma method the compound is heated with copper oxide and the nitrogen collected over KOH as N₂, whose volume gives the percentage of nitrogen. In the Kjeldahl method the nitrogen of the compound is converted to ammonium sulphate, made alkaline and distilled into standard acid, and the back-titration gives the nitrogen content as %N = 1.4 × M × V / w, where M is the molarity, V the volume of acid in mL and w the mass of the sample in milligrams... expressed for mass in grams the same relation reads %N = 1400 × M × V / (1000 × w). In the Carius method the compound is heated with fuming nitric acid and silver nitrate so that halogen appears as silver halide, weighed to give the percentage of halogen. Carbon and hydrogen are estimated together by burning the compound in oxygen and absorbing the products in weighed alkali and perchloric acid traps; the mass gains give the percentages directly.

items.text: A 0.24 g organic compound gave 0.168 g of CO₂ and 0.072 g of water on combustion. Find the percentages of carbon and hydrogen.
items.note: Carbon in CO₂ = 12/44 × 0.168 = 0.0458 g, so %C = 0.0458/0.24 × 100 = 19.1%. Hydrogen in H₂O = 2/18 × 0.072 = 0.008 g, so %H = 0.008/0.24 × 100 = 3.3%. The remainder is the other element present, and the two percentages can then be converted to moles to find the empirical formula.

items.text: In the Carius method a 0.250 g sample of an organic compound containing bromine was heated with fuming nitric acid and silver nitrate, and the bromine was recovered as 0.356 g of silver bromide. Calculate the percentage of bromine in the compound.
items.note: The Carius method converts the halogen into the corresponding silver halide, so all the bromine in the sample ends up in AgBr. Molar mass of AgBr = 107.87 + 79.90 = 187.77 g mol⁻¹. Mass of bromine in 0.356 g of AgBr = 79.90 / 187.77 × 0.356 = 0.151 g. Percentage of bromine in the original sample = 0.151 / 0.250 × 100 = 60.4%. The calculation follows the same pattern for chlorine or iodine: find the mass of halogen in the weighed silver halide, divide by the sample mass and multiply by 100. The result should be checked as sensible - a value above 100% means the silver halide was weighed with more halogen than was present in the sample, usually because the compound was not pure or the sample mass was misread.

items: Choose the separation by property: melting point difference (crystallisation), volatility (distillation), sublimation or adsorption (chromatography).
A pure compound has a sharp, constant melting or boiling point; a broad range signals impurity.
Rf = distance moved by solute / distance moved by solvent, and it is characteristic for a given component.
Kjeldahl gives nitrogen as ammonia; the Duma method gives nitrogen as N₂ gas; the Carius method gives halogen as AgX.
Purity is confirmed before analysis, because every percentage calculation assumes the sample is the compound it is thought to be.

keyPoints: Carbon is tetravalent, small and catenate — the three properties behind the size of organic chemistry.
Hybridisation fixes shape: sp³ tetrahedral, sp² trigonal planar, sp linear.
Bond-line formulas imply carbon at every vertex and enough hydrogens to complete four bonds.
IUPAC: longest chain containing the principal group, lowest locants, alphabetical prefixes, prefix-root-suffix.
Structural isomers differ in connectivity; geometrical isomers differ in spatial arrangement about a restricted bond.
Homolytic fission gives radicals; heterolytic fission gives carbocations and carbanions.
Inductive is permanent and weak; resonance is permanent and strong; electromeric is temporary; hyperconjugation involves sigma bonds only.
Stability order of carbocations and alkenes: 3° > 2° > 1° > methyl, explained by hyperconjugation and +I.
Nucleophiles attack positive centres; electrophiles attack electron-rich sites.
Purification exploits differences in solubility, volatility or adsorption; purity is confirmed by a sharp melting or boiling point.
examFocus: This is the heaviest unit of the paper at 11 marks: expect IUPAC naming, isomer counting, and a mechanism or electron-displacement question every year.
Percentage-composition calculations from combustion, Kjeldahl or Carius data are the standard numerical; learn the constant 1.4 in the Kjeldahl expression.
State the effect being invoked explicitly (inductive, resonance, electromeric, hyperconjugation) and its direction — unnamed effects score poorly.

vocabulary.meaning: The atom or group responsible for the characteristic reactions of an organic family.
The systematic name assigned by International Union rules: prefix, root word and suffix.
One of two or more compounds with the same molecular formula but different structures.
The step-by-step sequence of bond breaking, electron movement and bond formation in a reaction.
An electron-rich species that donates an electron pair to an electron-deficient centre.
An electron-deficient species that accepts an electron pair from an electron-rich site.
Delocalisation of a sigma bond of an alkyl group into an adjacent p or π system.

questions.prompt: The IUPAC name of the compound CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃ is:
questions.explanation: The longest continuous chain has four carbons (butane), and numbering from the nearer end puts the methyl branch on carbon 2, giving 2-methylbutane. Option C is the common name rather than the IUPAC name, and option D is not a valid name because its parent chain would in fact be five carbons long.

questions.prompt: When a C–X bond in which X is the more electronegative atom undergoes heterolytic fission, the carbon atom becomes:
questions.explanation: Both electrons of the shared pair go to the electronegative X, which leaves carrying a negative charge as X⁻. The carbon atom has lost its share of the pair, so it carries a positive charge and is a carbocation — the electron-deficient intermediate that nucleophiles attack. A carbanion would form only if carbon took both electrons, and a free radical only from homolytic fission.

questions.prompt: The number of structural isomers of C₄H₁₀ is:
questions.explanation: Butane and 2-methylpropane are the only two ways of arranging four carbon atoms with the formula C₄H₁₀: a straight chain and a branched chain. Both are saturated, so no position or functional isomers are possible.

questions.prompt: Which electron-displacement effect is responsible for the greater stability of a tertiary carbocation compared with a primary one?
questions.explanation: A tertiary carbocation has alkyl groups whose C–H sigma bonds can overlap with the empty p orbital of the positively charged carbon, delocalising the positive charge over several atoms. This is hyperconjugation: the more alkyl groups attached to the cation centre, the more such interactions are possible, giving the order 3° > 2° > 1° > methyl.

questions.prompt: The number of covalent bonds formed by a carbon atom in its compounds is __________.
questions.explanation: Carbon has four valence electrons and completes its octet by forming four covalent bonds, which may be single, double or triple; this tetravalence, together with catenation, is why organic chemistry is so large.

questions.prompt: The separation technique used for a mixture of camphor and sand is __________.
questions.explanation: Camphor sublimes — it passes directly from solid to vapour on gentle heating — while sand is non-volatile, so heating the mixture leaves the sand behind and the camphor collects on the cool surface of the funnel.

questions.prompt: Define the terms chain isomerism and position isomerism with an example of each.
questions.answer: Chain isomerism is isomerism in which the carbon skeleton is arranged differently while the molecular formula and functional group stay the same: butane (CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃) and 2-methylpropane ((CH₃)₃CH) are chain isomers, both C₄H₁₀ alkanes. Position isomerism is isomerism in which the same functional group or multiple bond occupies a different position on the same skeleton: propan-1-ol (CH₃CH₂CH₂OH) and propan-2-ol (CH₃CH(OH)CH₃) are position isomers, both C₃H₈O alcohols.
questions.explanation: Both terms describe structural isomerism, and the distinction rests on whether the carbon skeleton itself changes or only the location of the group attached to it.

questions.prompt: Explain the inductive effect and state why its influence decreases with distance.
questions.answer: The inductive effect is the permanent polarisation of a sigma bond caused by the electronegativity difference between the bonded atoms, transmitted along the chain of sigma bonds from the substituent that causes it. An electronegative group such as chlorine pulls electron density towards itself, making the bond polar and inducing a smaller opposite polarity in the next bond, and so on. The effect weakens with distance because each successive bond only partially transmits the displacement and the induced dipoles are progressively smaller, so the effect is generally considered negligible beyond three or four carbon atoms from the substituent.
questions.explanation: Marks here go to three points: the effect is permanent, it operates through sigma bonds, and it falls off rapidly with the number of bonds separating it from the site being affected.

questions.prompt: Describe the purification of a solid organic compound by crystallisation and state how the purity of the crystals is then checked.
questions.answer: Crystallisation depends on the difference in solubility between the compound and its impurities, and on the fall in solubility with temperature. The impure solid is dissolved in the minimum volume of a suitable solvent at a temperature close to its boiling point, so that a hot saturated solution forms; insoluble impurities are then removed by hot gravity filtration. The filtrate is allowed to cool slowly, and as the solution becomes supersaturated the pure compound crystallises out, leaving the soluble impurities behind in the mother liquor. If the crystals are small or contaminated the process is repeated, a technique called recrystallisation, and the crystals are filtered off, washed with a little cold solvent and dried. Purity is then checked by measuring the melting point: a pure compound melts sharply at a single temperature, whereas even a few per cent of impurity depresses and broadens the melting range, so a range of more than one or two degrees indicates that the crystals are not pure.
questions.explanation: The answer must link the technique to the property being exploited — differential solubility — and end with the standard purity test, since the question asks for both the separation and its verification.

questions.prompt: A 0.500 g sample of an organic compound containing only carbon, hydrogen and nitrogen was analysed by the Kjeldahl method. The ammonia produced was absorbed in 50 mL of 0.5 M HCl, and the acid left over required 45 mL of 0.5 M NaOH for neutralisation. Calculate the percentage of nitrogen in the compound.
questions.answer: The Kjeldahl method converts every nitrogen atom of the compound into ammonium sulphate, which on making alkaline releases NH₃; the ammonia is distilled into a known excess of standard acid and the surplus acid is found by back-titration. Millimoles of acid taken = 50 × 0.5 = 25.0. Millimoles of acid remaining = millimoles of NaOH used = 45 × 0.5 = 22.5. Millimoles of acid neutralised by ammonia = 25.0 − 22.5 = 2.5, and since each NH₃ consumes one H⁺, this equals the millimoles of nitrogen. Mass of nitrogen = 2.5 × 14 = 35 mg = 0.035 g. Percentage of nitrogen = 0.035/0.500 × 100 = 7.0%. The general working is %N = 1.4 × M × V / w with V in millilitres and w in milligrams when a single standard is used, and the answer must always be checked as sensible, since a value above 100% means the volumes or the sample mass have been misread.
questions.explanation: Marks are awarded for the three-step chain — acid taken, acid left, acid consumed — and for converting millimoles of ammonia into millimoles of nitrogen, because one mole of NH₃ carries exactly one mole of N.
